

This vignette covers the forecasting functions of arimatools. Point forecasts
come from `forecast::forecast()`. Forecast uncertainty is built from the
$\psi$-weights of the fitted model, so that the shape of the forecast and
the growth of its uncertainty can be traced back to the model:

- `dynamic_forecast()` returns forecasts, forecast-error variances and intervals as a table;
- `forecast_error_variance()` and `dynamic_effects()` expose the $\psi$-weights behind them;
- `plot_forecast()` and `plot_fan_chart()` draw them.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(forecast)
library(arimatools)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Dynamic forecasts

At the forecast origin $T$, future innovations have conditional expectation
zero and future observations are replaced by their forecasts. For an AR(1),

$$
\hat y_{T+h|T} = \hat\phi^h y_T .
$$

```{r}
set.seed(1010)
y_ar1 <- arima.sim(list(ar = 0.75), n = 250, n.start = 200)
fit_ar1 <- Arima(y_ar1, order = c(1, 0, 0), include.mean = FALSE)

fc <- dynamic_forecast(fit_ar1, steps = 6, level = 0.95)
fc
all.equal(fc$forecast, coef(fit_ar1)[["ar1"]]^(1:6) * as.numeric(tail(y_ar1, 1)))
```

These are single-origin forecasts: every horizon is made from the end of the
sample, and the model is not re-estimated as new observations arrive.

```{r}
plot_forecast(fit_ar1, steps = 12, history = 40)
```

## The $\psi$-weights explain the forecast

Writing the model as an MA($\infty$), $y_t = \sum_{j \ge 0}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}$,
the known innovations affect $\hat y_{T+h|T}$ only through
$\psi_h, \psi_{h+1}, \dots$: the forecast dies out as fast as the weights do.
`dynamic_effects()` returns the weights and their cumulative sum.

```{r}
set.seed(22)
fit_ma2 <- Arima(arima.sim(list(ma = c(0.70, 0.35)), n = 250),
                 order = c(0, 0, 2), include.mean = FALSE)
set.seed(33)
fit_arma11 <- Arima(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.70, ma = 0.45), n = 250),
                    order = c(1, 0, 1), include.mean = FALSE)

dynamic_effects(fit_ma2, horizon = 5)
```

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plot_dynamic_effects(fit_arma11, horizon = 12, title = "ARMA(1,1): psi-weights")
```

For integrated models the weights include the differencing polynomial, so
they are responses of the level and need not decay.

## Forecast uncertainty

The forecast-error variance at horizon $h$ is

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(y_{T+h} - \hat y_{T+h|T}\right) = \sigma^2 \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} \psi_j^2 .
$$

For a stationary model it converges to the unconditional variance of $y_t$.

```{r}
fev <- forecast_error_variance(fit_arma11, steps = 40)
long_run <- fit_arma11$sigma2 * sum(dynamic_effects(fit_arma11, 2000)$effect^2)
c(h1 = fev[1], h40 = fev[40], unconditional = long_run)
```

A fan chart displays several central prediction intervals at once.

```{r}
plot_fan_chart(fit_arma11, steps = 25, levels = c(0.50, 0.80, 0.95), history = 60)
```

### Comparison with the Kalman filter

`forecast::forecast()` computes the same intervals with the Kalman filter.
For a complete sample and an invertible MA part, the two coincide:

```{r}
kf <- forecast(fit_arma11, h = 25, level = 95)
max(abs(dynamic_forecast(fit_arma11, 25)$upper - kf$upper[, 1]))
```

Neither includes parameter or model-selection uncertainty: both treat the
estimated model as known.

The $\psi$-weight variances assume that past innovations are known. That
fails when the MA polynomial has a root on the unit circle, typically after
overdifferencing. arimatools then warns, because its intervals would be
narrower than the Kalman ones:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
y_rw <- ts(cumsum(rnorm(120)), frequency = 12)
fit_over <- suppressWarnings(Arima(y_rw, order = c(0, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1)))
fev_over <- forecast_error_variance(fit_over, 12)
```

## Integration changes the forecast

With one unit root, shocks are permanent: the random-walk forecast is
$\hat y_{T+h|T} = y_T$. A constant in the differenced equation,
$\Delta y_t = c + \varepsilon_t$, becomes a linear drift in the level
forecast, $\hat y_{T+h|T} = y_T + hc$.

```{r}
set.seed(606)
y_i1 <- ts(cumsum(0.15 + rnorm(220)))
fit_i1 <- Arima(y_i1, order = c(0, 1, 0), include.drift = TRUE)
plot_fan_chart(fit_i1, steps = 30, levels = c(0.50, 0.80, 0.95), history = 80)
```

With two unit roots, $\Delta^2 y_t = \varepsilon_t$, the current slope
persists: $\hat y_{T+h|T} = y_T + h\,\Delta y_T$, a linear forecast without
any deterministic term.

```{r}
set.seed(707)
y_i2 <- ts(cumsum(cumsum(rnorm(220, sd = 0.3))))
fit_i2 <- Arima(y_i2, order = c(0, 2, 0))
plot_fan_chart(fit_i2, steps = 30, levels = c(0.50, 0.80, 0.95), history = 80)
```

The $\psi$-weights die out for $d = 0$, are constant for $d = 1$, and grow
linearly for $d = 2$. Relative to $\sigma^2$, the forecast-error variance
therefore converges, grows like $h$, or grows like $h^3$:

```{r}
fit_rw <- Arima(ts(cumsum(rnorm(220))), order = c(0, 1, 0))
h <- 30
ratios <- rbind(
  data.frame(h = 1:h, ratio = forecast_error_variance(fit_arma11, h) / fit_arma11$sigma2,
             model = "d = 0: ARMA(1,1)"),
  data.frame(h = 1:h, ratio = forecast_error_variance(fit_rw, h) / fit_rw$sigma2,
             model = "d = 1: random walk"),
  data.frame(h = 1:h, ratio = forecast_error_variance(fit_i2, h) / fit_i2$sigma2,
             model = "d = 2")
)
ggplot(ratios, aes(h, ratio, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Horizon", y = "FEV / sigma^2 (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Models with regressors

The arimatools forecasting functions handle a mean or a drift. Models with
other regressors need their future values, and are left to
`forecast::forecast(fit, xreg = ...)`; `dynamic_forecast()` says so.

A constant in the second-difference equation, which `forecast::Arima()`
does not allow with $d = 2$, can be supplied as the regressor
$x_t = t^2/2$, whose second difference is one:

```{r, error = TRUE}
set.seed(808)
n2 <- 220
y_i2c <- ts(cumsum(cumsum(0.025 + rnorm(n2, sd = 0.25))))
x <- (1:n2)^2 / 2
fit_i2c <- Arima(y_i2c, order = c(0, 2, 0), xreg = x)
dynamic_forecast(fit_i2c, 30)
```

```{r}
fc_i2c <- forecast(fit_i2c, xreg = ((n2 + 1):(n2 + 30))^2 / 2, level = c(50, 80, 95))
autoplot(fc_i2c, include = 80) + theme_minimal()
```

### Forecasting after an intervention

The same applies to intervention models built with `outlier_regressors()`.
An additive outlier close to the forecast origin distorts the estimated
dynamics and the forecast; modeling it explicitly protects both.

```{r}
set.seed(909)
u <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.4), n = 240))
y_out <- ts(u); y_out[233] <- y_out[233] + 8

X_ao <- outlier_regressors(y_out, positions = 233, types = "AO")
fit_int <- Arima(y_out, order = c(1, 0, 1), xreg = X_ao, include.mean = FALSE)
```

To forecast, supply the future values of the intervention regressor, with
the same column name as in estimation:

| Intervention | Future values $X_{T+1}, X_{T+2}, \dots$ |
|---|---|
| Additive outlier (AO) | $0, 0, 0, \dots$ |
| Level shift (LS) | $1, 1, 1, \dots$ |
| Temporary change (TC) | $\delta^{T+1-t_0}, \delta^{T+2-t_0}, \dots$ |

```{r}
h <- 20
X_future <- matrix(0, nrow = h, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(X_ao)))
fc_int <- forecast(fit_int, xreg = X_future, level = c(50, 80, 95))
autoplot(fc_int, include = 60) + theme_minimal()
```

The meaning of the intervention must therefore be specified before
forecasting, since it determines the future values of the regressor.
